approved: Introduced the Amending Acts 1901 to 1969 Repeal Bill 2014, which removes more than 1,000 spent amending and repeal acts to simplify the statute book, citing the Defence Act 1904 as the earliest being repealed and the long-obsolete Dried Fruits Export Charges Act 1927 as an example of redundant legislation.

Moved to suspend standing orders to fast-track the Omnibus Repeal Day (Autumn 2014) Bill 2014 and related repeal bills, setting a second reading debate deadline of 5.30 pm and capping the consideration in detail stage at 60 minutes. Said the government intended to pass the bills by the end of the day.

Mocked the statute law revision bill as trivial housekeeping dressed up as reform, citing changes such as replacing the hyphenated 'e-mail' with 'email' and fixing a spelling error in the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act. Challenged the government to justify its claim that repeal day would save more than $700 million a year by scrapping 9,500 regulations and 1,000 redundant acts.

Argued the amending acts repeal bill changes nothing, noting the Commonwealth Star's size has been unchanged for 60 years despite the repeal of the amending act. Said the former Labor government repealed 16,794 acts and instruments while delivering real reforms, and warned that unwinding the Future of Financial Advice laws risked a repeat of the Storm Financial collapse.

Said Telstra will no longer need to provide 70,000 pages of wholesale contracts to the ACCC under the reforms, which deliver a $720 million pay-off by removing more than 10,000 redundant regulations, and noted Australia ranked a lowly 128th out of 148 countries for regulatory burden under Labor.

Challenged the member for Kooyong to identify any actual savings to Australian businesses or individuals from the Amending Acts 1901 to 1969 Repeal Bill, which repeals 1,120 spent acts, and the Statute Law Revision Bill, which he said mainly corrects hyphens, commas and spelling errors.

Answered questions from the day's repeal debate, citing $0.21 million and $0.35 million in annual compliance savings from two repeal bills, and said the previous government's 21,000 additional regulations left Australia ranked 128th out of 148 countries for regulatory burden.
